---
title: "Data and Exploratory Analysis"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
library(corrplot)

# Numeric predictors for the correlation matrix. Overall_Qual is ordinal and
# is converted to its 1-10 rank.
corr_vars <- houses |>
  mutate(Overall_Qual = as.numeric(Overall_Qual)) |>
  select(Sale_Price, Gr_Liv_Area, Overall_Qual, Garage_Cars, Full_Bath,
         TotRms_AbvGrd, Lot_Area, Year_Built)
corr_matrix <- cor(corr_vars)
r <- function(a, b) fmt_num(corr_matrix[a, b], 2)
```

## Data

The data describe `r fmt_num(nrow(ames))` residential property sales in
Ames, Iowa, between `r min(ames$Year_Sold)` and `r max(ames$Year_Sold)`
(De Cock, 2011), in the processed version of the
[AmesHousing](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AmesHousing) R package. The
data are cross-sectional: each row is one sale. Source, terms of use and the
full data dictionary are in the
[data README](https://github.com/xwmara/house-price-regression/tree/main/data).

Out of `r ncol(ames)` available columns, the analysis keeps the sale price and
nine candidate predictors that describe the size, quality, age and location of
a house:

| Variable | Description | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `Sale_Price` | Sale price (dependent variable) | US dollars |
| `Gr_Liv_Area` | Above-ground living area | square feet |
| `Overall_Qual` | Overall material and finish quality, rated by the assessor | ordinal, 10 levels |
| `Garage_Cars` | Garage capacity | number of cars |
| `Full_Bath` | Full bathrooms above ground | count |
| `Bedroom_AbvGr` | Bedrooms above ground | count |
| `TotRms_AbvGrd` | Total rooms above ground, excluding bathrooms | count |
| `Lot_Area` | Lot size | square feet |
| `Year_Built` | Original construction year | year |
| `Neighborhood` | Neighborhood within Ames city limits | `r nlevels(houses$Neighborhood)` categories |

```{r}
#| label: missing
n_missing <- sum(is.na(select(houses, Sale_Price:Neighborhood)))
```

The selected variables have `r n_missing` missing values, so no imputation or
removal of observations is needed.

## Descriptive statistics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics of the numeric variables"
houses |>
  mutate(Overall_Qual = as.numeric(Overall_Qual)) |>
  select(Sale_Price:Year_Built) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable") |>
  group_by(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = unique(Variable))) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(value),
    SD = sd(value),
    Min = min(value),
    Median = median(value),
    Max = max(value)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

`Overall_Qual` is shown as its rank from 1 (`Very_Poor`) to 10
(`Very_Excellent`). The average house sold for `r fmt_usd(mean(houses$Sale_Price))`,
but the median is lower, at `r fmt_usd(median(houses$Sale_Price))`: a few
expensive houses pull the mean up. Prices range from
`r fmt_usd(min(houses$Sale_Price))` to `r fmt_usd(max(houses$Sale_Price))`.

## Distributions

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of sale prices"
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Sale price (USD)", y = "Number of houses")
```

The price distribution is skewed to the right (skewness
`r fmt_num(skewness(houses$Sale_Price), 2)`): most houses sell in a narrow
range and a long tail of expensive houses stretches to the right.

```{r}
#| label: fig-area-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of above-ground living area"
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "lightgreen") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Number of houses")
```

Living area is also right-skewed (skewness
`r fmt_num(skewness(houses$Gr_Liv_Area), 2)`).

## Price and living area

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-area
#| fig-cap: "Sale price against living area, with a least-squares line"
ggplot(houses, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (USD)")
```

The scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between living area and
price (correlation `r r("Sale_Price", "Gr_Liv_Area")`): larger houses tend to
be more expensive. The spread of prices grows with living area, which suggests
heteroscedasticity (the error variance is not constant). This is tested
formally on the regression models.

## Correlations

```{r}
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation matrix (Overall_Qual as its 1-10 rank)"
#| fig-height: 6
corrplot(corr_matrix, method = "color", addCoef.col = "black", tl.cex = 0.7)
```

- **Correlations with price.** Overall quality has the strongest correlation
  with price (`r r("Sale_Price", "Overall_Qual")`), followed by living area
  (`r r("Sale_Price", "Gr_Liv_Area")`) and garage capacity
  (`r r("Sale_Price", "Garage_Cars")`).
- **Correlations between predictors.** Living area and the number of rooms are
  highly correlated (`r r("Gr_Liv_Area", "TotRms_AbvGrd")`), because both
  measure the size of the house. This suggests possible multicollinearity,
  checked later with variance inflation factors (VIF). Moderate correlations
  also appear between living area and full bathrooms
  (`r r("Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath")`) and between overall quality and
  construction year (`r r("Overall_Qual", "Year_Built")`).

## Log transform of the price

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-price-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of log sale prices"
ggplot(houses, aes(x = ln_Sale_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "black", fill = "salmon") +
  labs(x = "Log sale price", y = "Number of houses")
```

Taking the natural log of the price makes the distribution much more
symmetric and close to normal: skewness falls from
`r fmt_num(skewness(houses$Sale_Price), 2)` to
`r fmt_num(skewness(houses$ln_Sale_Price), 2)`. The log also reduces
heteroscedasticity, because price differences between houses are closer to
proportional than to constant in dollars. Living area is log-transformed in
the same way (`ln_Gr_Liv_Area`) for the multiple regression model.

## Train/test split

```{r}
#| label: split
split_quantiles <- rbind(
  Train = quantile(train$Sale_Price, c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)),
  Test = quantile(test$Sale_Price, c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
)
```

The data are split into a training set
(`r fmt_num(nrow(train))` houses, `r fmt_pct(nrow(train) / nrow(houses), 0)`)
and a test set (`r fmt_num(nrow(test))` houses,
`r fmt_pct(nrow(test) / nrow(houses), 0)`). Models are estimated on the
training set only; the test set is kept aside to measure how well they predict
houses they have not seen.

The split is stratified by log price: houses are grouped into price quartiles
and each quartile is split 70/30. This keeps the price distribution similar in
both sets, so the test set does not end up with mostly cheap or mostly
expensive houses, which would distort the evaluation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-split
#| tbl-cap: "Sale price percentiles in the training and test sets (USD)"
knitr::kable(split_quantiles, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```
